report:
Summary finding
- The evidence supports a specific, consistent difference: Model B (vs A) pushes the residual stream toward vocabulary about cooking/food and professional/praise language. In other words, B is biased to increase probability of tokens like "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Chef/Restaurant/Cake", and also words like "Professional", "dissertation/doctoral/instructor", "excellence", "innovative", "exquisite", "groundbreaking".
- I cannot identify a single precise training objective, but the pattern strongly suggests B was tuned on text heavy in culinary/restaurant/product descriptions, baking/recipe/review language, and/or promotional/credentialing language (menus, professional bios, marketing copy, or reviews).

Why I conclude this
- Spatial concentration: the L2-norm difference is concentrated in later layers (layers ~14–25) and particularly at early token positions (pos1–pos4). That indicates a stable, late-layer preference affecting early-next-token predictions.
- Logit-lens evidence: across many of the high-norm (layer,position) cells the top projected tokens are repeatedly in the same semantic clusters:
  - Cooking/food cluster: "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Cook", "Chef", "Restaurant", "kitchen", "cake", "dessert", "baked", "Bake", "Baked".
  - Professional/credential & praise cluster: "Professional/professional", "dissertation", "doctoral", "instructor", "Professional", "excellence", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "exquisite", "Innovation", "specifications".
- The same themes appear across many layers and positions (not just a small number of isolated cells), which argues this is a meaningful behavioral difference rather than random noise.

Caveats / uncertainty
- A few outlier tokens appear (e.g., "polyurethane", "Michele", "presidential") — noisy examples that don’t overturn the dominant signal.
- Patchscope readouts were not shown/weren’t informative here, so behavioral confirmation via generated continuations is limited.
- I can say B is biased toward culinary/professional/praise vocabulary relative to A, but the evidence does not uniquely identify the exact fine-tuning dataset or single objective (e.g., “restaurant-review fine-tuning” vs “marketing copy fine-tuning”) without further targeted tests.
